name: Alex T - May 5
transcript:
Therapist: Alex, how are you today?

Alex: Honestly? Angry. I had another fight with my dad this weekend and I'm still stewing about it.

Therapist: Tell me what happened.

Alex: Same old pattern. We were at family dinner and he made this comment about my career, like a backhanded compliment about how nice it must be to have a job that's not too stressful. Implying what I do isn't real work because I'm a designer and not a lawyer like him.

Therapist: How did you respond in the moment?

Alex: I didn't. I just went quiet and then left early. My mom texted me later saying I was being rude by leaving.

Therapist: So you're dealing with the initial invalidation from your father and then a secondary one from your mother framing your response as the problem.

Alex: Yes! Exactly! I'm always the one who's being too sensitive or making a big deal out of nothing. But his comments actually hurt and I'm tired of pretending they don't.

Therapist: Your feelings are valid. His comments are dismissive of your chosen career and by extension your identity. Last time we talked about the difference between reacting and responding. Let's revisit that. When he made the comment, what was happening in your body?

Alex: My chest got tight and my face got hot. I could feel myself wanting to either explode or disappear. So I chose disappear.

Therapist: Fight or flight. Both are stress responses. You chose flight, which protected you from escalation but left the issue unaddressed. What would a response look like, as opposed to a reaction?

Alex: I guess something like... Dad, when you say things like that it feels like you don't value what I do. I'd appreciate it if you didn't make jokes about my career.

Therapist: That's a very clear, non-aggressive boundary statement. What stops you from saying something like that in the moment?

Alex: Fear, probably. I'm thirty-two years old and I'm still afraid of my dad's disapproval. It's pathetic.

Therapist: It's not pathetic. It's developmental. We're wired to seek parental approval. The work isn't about not wanting it anymore but about not needing it to validate your self-worth. Do you feel proud of your career independent of his opinion?

Alex: Most of the time, yes. I love what I do. I'm good at it. I just won a design award last month. But then I'm around him and suddenly I'm fifteen again trying to justify why I want to go to art school instead of pre-law.

Therapist: That regression is so common in family systems. The old dynamics have deep grooves. One thing I want to explore is: what would it mean for you if your dad never validates your career? If that approval never comes?

Alex: I don't know. I think part of me is still waiting for it. Like if I just succeed enough, eventually he'll get it.

Therapist: And that waiting, that hoping, does it serve you or does it keep you stuck?

Alex: It keeps me stuck. Because even when good things happen, there's always this voice saying yeah but dad wouldn't be impressed.

Therapist: So the internal critic has his voice. That's something we can work with. When you hear that voice, I want you to practice noticing it and labeling it. That's my dad's voice, not my voice. My voice says I'm proud of this work.

Alex: That feels weird but I'll try it.

Therapist: It will feel weird at first. It's a new neural pathway. Give it a few weeks. And regarding the family dinners, would it help to prepare in advance? Knowing that comments might come and having a planned response ready?

Alex: Like a script?

Therapist: More like a couple of prepared phrases you can reach for when your stress response activates. So you have an alternative to silence or explosion.

Alex: Yeah, that could work. Can we practice that?

Therapist: Absolutely. Let's role play. I'll be your dad. Ready?

Alex: This is going to be weird. Okay, go.

Therapist: So Alex, must be nice having all that free time at your job to be creative. Wish I could draw pictures for a living.

Alex: Dad, I love my work and I'm successful at it. I'd rather we talked about something else.

Therapist: How did that feel?

Alex: Terrifying. But also good? Like, short and clear. Not mean, not apologetic.

Therapist: Perfect. Direct, boundaried, and you don't engage with the content of his jab. You redirect. That's a skill and you just demonstrated it.

Alex: Okay. I can work with this. Next dinner is in two weeks. I'll be ready.

Therapist: Good. And remember, even if you freeze in the moment again, that's okay. This is a practice, not a test. Same time next week?

Alex: Yes. Thanks. I feel less angry already just having said it out loud.
